headline: Employer costs for employee compensation averaged $49.46 per hour worked in June

items.title: Employer Costs for Employee Compensation, June 2026
items.summary: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that employer costs for employee compensation for civilian workers averaged $49.46 per hour worked in June 2026, made up of $33.85 in wages and salaries and $15.61 in benefits. In private industry, compensation averaged $46.89 per hour, with wages and salaries accounting for 70.0 percent of costs and benefits for 30.0 percent. For state and local government workers the average was $66.45 per hour, of which benefits made up 38.8 percent.
items.meaning: This measure counts what employers spend per hour worked on pay and on benefits, including paid leave, supplemental pay, insurance, retirement and savings, and legally required benefits. For civilian workers, benefits were 31.6 percent of total compensation in June, so a comparison based on wages alone leaves out close to a third of employer costs.

items.title: Quarterly Services Survey, second quarter 2026
items.summary: The Census Bureau reported that revenue for U.S. selected services industries totaled $6,418.7 billion in the second quarter of 2026, adjusted for seasonal variation but not for price changes. That was 3.0 percent above the first quarter of 2026 and 7.6 percent above the second quarter of 2025. The change from the first quarter was revised from the advance estimate of 3.1 percent.
items.meaning: Revenue is measured in dollars without adjusting for prices, so an increase can reflect higher prices as well as more services sold. Because the figures come from a survey, each change is printed with a 90 percent confidence interval, here 3.0 percent plus or minus 0.4 percent.

sections.title: One concept to know
sections.conceptTitle: Margins of error in survey estimates
sections.text: Figures from a survey rather than a complete count carry sampling error, and the Census Bureau prints that uncertainty next to its estimates: services revenue rose 3.0 percent in the second quarter, plus or minus 0.4 percent, at 90 percent confidence. When such an interval includes zero, the Bureau states that there is insufficient evidence to conclude the actual change differs from zero.
